title: 3 Days in Bangkok: What You Actually Have to See
titleTag: 3 Days in Bangkok: The Must-See Itinerary
ogTitle: 3 Days in Bangkok — The Must-See Itinerary
metaDescription: The essential three-day Bangkok itinerary: the Grand Palace, Wat Pho, Wat Arun, Chinatown and the markets, ordered so heat and traffic cost you the least.
secondaryQueries: what to do in bangkok in 3 days
what to see in bangkok in 3 days
standfirst: Three days is enough for Bangkok's essentials, but only if you stop treating it as a walking city. Here is what genuinely has to be on the list, in the order that keeps you out of the worst heat and the worst traffic.
cardSummary: The Grand Palace, Wat Pho, Wat Arun and Chinatown — what to see and what to skip.

heroImage.alt: The porcelain-encrusted central prang of Wat Arun rising against a clear blue sky
heroImage.caption: Wat Arun's central prang. Close up, the whole surface turns out to be broken plates set into plaster.

body: Three days covers Bangkok's essentials comfortably: the royal temples in Rattanakosin, the river and Chinatown, and the markets. What it does not cover is Ayutthaya, which needs a full day of its own and is the thing most three-day itineraries wrongly try to squeeze in.

The plan below groups everything by neighbourhood and by time of day. Bangkok is flat, so the enemy here is not gradient. It is heat and traffic. A three-kilometre taxi ride at six in the evening can take longer than the same trip by boat, and the difference between a well-ordered day and a badly ordered one is roughly two hours sitting still in a car.

**The clock sets the order, not the map.** The Grand Palace stops selling tickets in mid-afternoon, currently 3.30pm, and by eleven in the morning it is the hottest and most crowded place you will stand all trip. It is the only stop with a hard deadline, so it goes first.

sections.heading: Day 1 — The Grand Palace, Wat Pho and Wat Arun
body: These three sit within a few minutes of each other in Rattanakosin, the old royal island, and they are the only part of the trip you can genuinely do on foot. Take them in order: palace, then Wat Pho, then across the river to Wat Arun. The day runs downhill from the crowds into the quiet.

**Dress properly or you will not get in.** The Grand Palace enforces the strictest dress code in Thailand, and it enforces it at the gate: shoulders covered, knees covered, no shorts, no sleeveless tops, no ripped jeans. There is a place to cover up on site, but it is another queue in the sun. Wear long trousers or a long skirt and bring a light shirt with sleeves.

sections.alt: The golden chedi and tiered orange roofs of Wat Phra Kaew inside the Grand Palace complex
sections.caption: Wat Phra Kaew, inside the Grand Palace walls. The Emerald Buddha itself is small and set high above the floor. The complex around it is the spectacle.

sections.heading: The must-sees
sections.note: Dress for the palace before you leave the hotel. The rest of the day is walkable from one end to the other.

stops.name: Grand Palace and Wat Phra Kaew
stops.detail: Go at opening. By late morning the courtyards are full and there is no shade in them. Tickets stop being sold mid-afternoon, so this cannot be the afternoon stop.

stops.name: Wat Pho
stops.detail: A few minutes' walk south, and the better temple of the two. The reclining Buddha fills its hall so completely you cannot get it in one photograph.

stops.name: The Tha Tien cross-river ferry
stops.detail: The shuttle from the pier behind Wat Pho to the far bank. It costs almost nothing and is over almost before it starts, and it beats every tourist boat tied up beside it.

stops.name: Wat Arun
stops.detail: Close up, the prangs are covered in broken porcelain pressed into the plaster. The stairs up the central tower are genuinely steep. Climb them in the late-afternoon light.

stops.name: The river at sunset
stops.detail: Ferry back and eat on the Rattanakosin bank looking at Wat Arun lit up, which is the view worth staying out for.

sections.alt: The gold-leafed reclining Buddha at Wat Pho stretching the length of its pillared hall
sections.caption: The reclining Buddha at Wat Pho. The hall was built around it, which is why you can never quite step back far enough.

sections.heading: Day 2 — The river, the Golden Mount and Chinatown
body: Use the Chao Phraya express boats as transport, not as a tour. The orange-flag service runs up and down the river all day, stops at most of the piers you want, and keeps moving while the roads above it do not.

This day ends after dark on purpose. Yaowarat, the main street of Chinatown, is a daytime traffic jam and a night-time food market, and the difference between the two is total. Do not go at four in the afternoon and conclude it is overrated.

sections.heading: The must-sees
sections.note: River first while it is cool, one climb in the middle, Chinatown once the lights are on.

stops.name: Chao Phraya express boat
stops.detail: Take the orange-flag boat a few piers in either direction. It is public transport rather than a cruise, and it costs a fraction of what the tour operators charge.

stops.name: Wat Saket (the Golden Mount)
stops.detail: A few hundred steps spiralling up an artificial hill to a gold chedi. It gives the clearest view over the old city, and almost nobody queues for it.

stops.name: Talat Noi
stops.detail: The lanes between Chinatown and the river, full of old shophouses and engine-part workshops. The one part of central Bangkok that rewards walking with no plan.

stops.name: Yaowarat after dark
stops.detail: The food comes out around sunset and the street stays busy late. Eat standing up, from several places, instead of sitting down in one.

sections.alt: Neon signs in Thai and Chinese crowding above traffic on Yaowarat Road in Bangkok's Chinatown at night
sections.caption: Yaowarat Road after dark. The same street at four in the afternoon is just traffic.

sections.heading: Day 3 — Markets and the modern city
body: This is the day that depends on your dates. Chatuchak, the enormous weekend market, opens on Friday evening and then runs all day Saturday and Sunday, and simply does not exist the rest of the week. If your three days fall Monday to Thursday, do not build a day around it, and do not let a blog talk you into a weekday substitute that is a fraction of the size.
The rest of the day is the modern city: the Skytrain, a park, air conditioning at the hottest hour. After two days of temples, the change of register is deliberate.

sections.heading: The must-sees
sections.note: Market in the morning if it is a weekend; Jim Thompson House instead if it is not.

stops.name: Chatuchak Weekend Market
stops.detail: Thousands of stalls in numbered sections, reachable by MRT and BTS. Go early. It is covered but not cooled, and by midday the aisles are solid.

stops.name: Jim Thompson House (weekdays)
stops.detail: The teak house of the American who revived Thai silk, kept as he left it. Small, shaded and guided, and the easiest hour of the trip on a hot day.

stops.name: Lumphini Park
stops.detail: The city's green middle, with monitor lizards in the lake. Somewhere to sit down that is not a mall.

stops.name: The BTS Skytrain
stops.detail: Worth one deliberate ride above the traffic. It is the fastest way across the new city and the only one with a view.

stops.name: A rooftop, or one last street meal
stops.detail: The skyline bars are real but formal and expensive. A night market dinner is the cheaper answer and usually the better one.

sections.heading: What three days does not cover
sections.intro: Cutting deliberately beats rushing. These need more time than you have:
items: **Ayutthaya** — a full day, not a half day. The old capital deserves better than a coach stop.
**A floating market done properly** — Amphawa in the evening, on a weekend, is worth it; the coach-park version is not.
**Thonburi's canals** — the other side of the river is a different city and needs an unhurried morning.
**Shopping as an activity** — the malls are enormous and will eat a day if you let them.
**Anywhere outside Bangkok** — the islands and the north are separate trips, not extensions of this one.

faqHeading: Common questions about 3 days in Bangkok

faq.a: For the city itself, yes. Three days covers the Grand Palace, Wat Pho and Wat Arun, the river and Chinatown, and the markets at a reasonable pace. It is not enough to add Ayutthaya properly, which needs a full day of its own.

faq.q: What are the must-see temples in Bangkok?
faq.a: Wat Phra Kaew inside the Grand Palace, Wat Pho for the reclining Buddha, and Wat Arun across the river are the three nobody should miss, and they can be done in a single day. Wat Saket, the Golden Mount, is the strongest addition after those, mostly for the view.

faq.q: What should I wear to the Grand Palace?
faq.a: Shoulders and knees covered, for men and women alike. Shorts, sleeveless tops, crop tops and ripped jeans are all turned away at the gate. Cover-ups are available on site but that means queueing twice, so it is easier to arrive dressed for it.

faq.q: Is Chatuchak market open every day?
faq.a: No. Chatuchak is a weekend market: it opens on Friday evening and runs all day Saturday and Sunday. If your trip falls midweek, plan Day 3 around Jim Thompson House and the modern city instead.

faq.q: Is the floating market worth it?
faq.a: Not the famous one. Damnoen Saduak is hours of travel each way for a market that now runs largely for tour groups. If you want a floating market and your dates allow it, Amphawa on a weekend evening is the honest version. On a three-day trip, skipping both costs you nothing.

faq.q: How do you get around Bangkok?
faq.a: River boats and rail, in that order. The orange-flag Chao Phraya express boat covers the old city and the temples; the BTS Skytrain and MRT cover the modern one. Taxis and tuk-tuks are fine late at night and a poor idea in the late afternoon, when the traffic can make them slower than the boat.

faq.q: How much does the Grand Palace cost?
faq.a: Around 500 baht for adults at the time of writing, which covers Wat Phra Kaew inside the same walls. It is the one properly priced ticket of the trip. Most other temples charge a small fraction of that, and several are free.
